doc.title: Charles Davis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, August 23, 1997

title: Rhythm and blues, honking and Chicago showmanship
summary: Clarence Henry and R&B, honking and walking the bar, audiences who knew records' solos.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: Did you ever do much rhythm & blues playing in your career?
Let’s see, my Alzheimer’s just kicked in. Let’s see, well Clarence Henry was rhythm & blues. Clarence Henry. I played with quite a few rhythm & blues during the course of my career coming up.
Did you ever feel you had to really do that honking tenor sax thing?

Well that was a part of growing up. There was a lot of honking. John Coltrane had to honk. A lot of people had to honk. That was a tradition — honking and walking the bar. Sometimes you were forced to do it. Sometimes you were forced to do it at gun point. That’s in Chicago sometimes, people put a gun on you because they knew the solos so you couldn’t fool them.
The audience knew the solos. They paid that much attention to the records. They’d get the records, everybody knew the solos. So I know this happened to quite a few different people.
That they wanted to hear what was ...

They wanted to hear what was on the record. If you didn’t know it then you had to go home and learn it you know. You couldn’t fool ‘em. People wanted to hear “Flyin’ Home,” they wanted to hear the solo. They didn’t want you — if you couldn’t play it then you’d get off of that.
They don’t teach that in school.

No, no, no, no, they don’t teach you that. And if they want you to walk the bar, they wanted you to walk the bar. You couldn’t say that wasn’t in your contract. It’s time to walk the bar, it’s time to walk the bar. That’s another thing, people wanted to see a show you know. When it was show time then you had to go out and put on a show, you couldn’t sit around and be that cool that you couldn’t put on a show saying that’s not my thing. So if it’s show time you get up and put on a show.
You want to get paid, you better do it.
Yeah. You may do it and don’t get paid. Guys put on a show laying on his back and playing the saxophone behind his back, anything to get through that scene.
Yeah. But that was the tradition during that time.
